title: Opening a Bank Account in Istanbul
excerpt: How to open a Turkish bank account as a foreigner in Istanbul: the tax number you need first, which documents actually get accepted, and why the branch you walk into matters more than the bank you choose.
bodyHtml:
Get your tax number first

Before any bank will talk to you, you need a Turkish tax number (vergi numarası). It is free, and you can apply online through the tax administration's portal rather than queuing at a tax office. Take the number seriously — it follows you through every piece of official business here.

Bring your passport. If you already have a residence permit, bring that too; several things get easier the moment you can show one.

The branch matters more than the bank

This is the part nobody tells you. Turkish banks give branches real discretion over foreign customers, so two branches of the same bank can give you two different answers on the same day with the same documents. One opens your account in forty minutes. Another asks for a residence permit with more months left on it than you have.

What actually helps:

  • Go to a branch in a neighbourhood with lots of foreign residents. They have done this a hundred times and have a process. A branch in a residential suburb may never have onboarded a foreigner.
  • Go early on a weekday. Account opening is slow, and a branch that is slammed at lunchtime will find reasons to send you away.
  • If a branch says no, that is information about the branch, not about you. Try another one before concluding you are ineligible.

What to bring

Expect to need your passport, your tax number, a Turkish mobile number, and proof of address. Many branches will ask for your residence permit. Some will open an account for tourists; many will not, and the ones that do may restrict what the account can do.

The Turkish mobile number is not optional in practice — banking here runs on SMS confirmation for nearly everything, so sort your SIM out first. That ordering trips a lot of people up: SIM, then tax number, then bank.

Once the account is open

You will get a debit card and an IBAN. A few habits worth forming:

  • Domestic transfers are instant and normal. Paying rent, splitting a dinner, paying a repair — people move money by IBAN constantly. Learn the three words the apps use: havale (a transfer inside the same bank), EFT (between banks, through the interbank system, not instant and not around the clock), and FAST — the Central Bank's separate instant system, which moves money between banks 24/7, weekends and holidays included, up to a per-transaction limit.
  • Keep the banking app's language in English if you want — most major banks support it, but set it up at the branch while someone is there to help.
  • Ask specifically about fees on foreign-currency accounts and incoming international transfers. If money arrives from abroad regularly, this is the question that saves you the most.

Getting money in from abroad

Incoming international wires work but can be slow and are sometimes held for documentation about the source of funds — this is normal compliance, not suspicion. Have an explanation and paperwork ready if the amount is large.

Rates and fees vary enough between banks and providers that it is worth asking around before you commit to one route for recurring transfers.

Before you go

Requirements shift, and they shift unevenly between banks. Check the current rules with the bank itself, and ask in the community which branches are currently onboarding foreigners smoothly — that answer changes over time and is genuinely local knowledge rather than something you can look up.
